                           MOTION TO DISMISS AND ANSWER OF
                             PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C.

       In accordance with Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission, 1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM) submits this answer in

response to the Complaint Requesting Fast-Track Processing of Monongahela Power Company

(Mon Power) filed on October 6, 2026. Mon Power’s Complaint is a fishing expedition without

substance. The Complaint does not allege a Tariff violation, but merely the suspicion of one. Even

though Mon Power has not identified a Tariff violation upon which any relief could be based, Mon

Power still asserts entitlement to discovery to determine if there is any basis to believe that PJM

violated its Tariff; if so, Mon Power then seeks retroactive relief for a locked-in, past period of

market performance in and around Winter Storm Fern through an unspecified mechanism, which

could include “refund, resettlement, uplift reallocation, congestion-cost reallocation, or another

targeted revenue-neutral mechanism that remedies the harm to Mon Power’s customers.” 2

       That relief should be denied. It is well settled that the Commission cannot grant retroactive

relief in the absence of a Tariff violation. 3 Indeed, the Commission is not required to order a

                                         BACKGROUND

        A.        Operating Agreement, Schedule 1 Section 1.10.1(d)

        Operating Agreement Schedule 1, section 1.10.1(d) sets forth PJM’s authority to advance

schedule generation resources, particularly in the expectation of emergency conditions. As

relevant, that provision states:

        If the Office of the Interconnection’s forecast for the next seven days projects a
        likelihood of Emergency conditions, the Office of the Interconnection may commit,
        for all or part of such seven day period, to the use of generation resources with
        notification or start-up times greater than one day as necessary in order to alleviate
        or mitigate such Emergency, in accordance with the Market Sellers’ offers for such
        units for such periods and the specifications in the PJM Manuals. 9

PJM first added this language to its Tariff as part of its compliance with Order No. 888, though

undiscussed in either PJM’s filing or the Commission’s order accepting PJM’s compliance filing.

        Operating Agreement Schedule 1, section 1.10.1A(f), further clarifies that a Market Seller

with less than a 24-hour start-up time “may submit a non-binding forecast of the price at which it

expects to offer a generation resource increment to the Office of the Interconnection over the next

seven days.” 10 By contrast, a Market Seller “shall submit a binding offer for energy, along with

scenario, “resources committed by the Office of the Interconnection will not receive Operating

Reserve Credits nor otherwise be made whole for its hours of operation for the duration of any

portion of such commitment that exceeds the maximum start-up and notification times for such

resources during Hot Weather Alerts and Cold Weather Alerts, consistent with Operating

Agreement, Schedule 1, section 3.2.3 and Operating Agreement, Schedule 1, section 6.6.” 12 As

such, PJM was well within its rights and obligations under the Tariff to perform the advance

scheduling conducted prior to and during Winter Storm Fern.

       B.        Order No. 844

       In 2018, the Commission issued Order No. 844 to revise its regulations to improve

       resource name and total amount of uplift paid in dollars, aggregated across the

       post a monthly Operator-Initiated Commitment Report listing the commitment size,
       transmission zone, commitment reason, and commitment start time of each
       operator-initiated commitment.      Further, each RTO/ISO must follow the
       transmission constraint penalty factor requirements to include, in its tariff, its
       transmission constraint penalty factor values; the circumstances, if any, under

       C.         2025 Transmittal Letter

       In 2025, PJM submitted proposed revisions to its Operating Agreement and Tariff to update

its existing energy market rules so that PJM would only commit resources scheduled in advance

of the Day-ahead Market using their cost-based offers. 21 That proposal was meant to eliminate

the potential for Market Sellers of advance scheduled resources to increase their market-based

offer to a level that did not accurately reflect the costs associated with operating that resource when

evaluated in the clearing of the energy markets. 22 As part of the 2025 Transmittal Letter, PJM

explained that:

       Prior to 2024, PJM rarely pre-scheduled resources before the close of the Day-
       ahead Energy Market and did so primarily to address projected transmission
       constraints. That practice changed in recent years in response to lessons learned
       from Winter Storm Elliott when certain gas-fired resources were not able to procure
       natural gas after receiving commitments in the Day ahead Energy Market or Real-
       time Energy Market due, in part, to the timing of gas nomination cycles and
       relatively illiquid gas market leading into and over long holiday weekends. To
       prudently operate the grid and prospectively mitigate against the risk of fuel
       procurement issues, PJM now pre-schedules resources in advance of the Day-ahead
       Energy Market more frequently when Emergency conditions may be anticipated.
       Specifically, PJM may pre-schedule resources up to seven days in advance of the
       Day-ahead Energy Market when PJM’s forecast “projects a likelihood of
       Emergency conditions.” 23

         E.         PJM and Other RTOs/ISOs Followed the Department of Energy’s Lead in
                   Treating the Storm as a Serious Emergency

        PJM was not alone in treating Winter Storm Fern with appropriate seriousness. During

Winter Storm Fern and the other winter weather events occurring at that time, the Secretary of

Energy determined that a statutory emergency existed and issued emergency orders that:

(1) directed electric entities to dispatch certain units only as needed to maintain reliability, which

allowed generators to exceed Federal, State, or Local environmental limitations; and (2) authorized

electric entities to direct backup generation resources at data centers and other large load industrial

and commercial customer sites to operate as a last resort. 42 The Secretary of Energy also directed

the continued operation of certain generators slated for retirement. Specifically, the Secretary of

Energy issued a total of fifteen FPA section 202(c) emergency orders and five extension orders,

including to PJM, over the course of the Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period. 43 In PJM, the

Department of Energy’s orders resulted in 39 units with a total of 5,704 MW of capacity providing

271,150 MWh of energy that otherwise would have been precluded from operating. 44 The

Department of Energy also held conference calls with reliability coordinators, balancing

authorities, and others prior to the winter storms. 45

        Like PJM, other RTOs/ISOs took urgent action to strengthen their systems. ERCOT,

MISO, PJM, SPP, TVA, and VACAR South all brought in additional operators and staff engineers

to ensure their control centers were adequately staffed during the prolonged arctic cold period. 46

                                       MOTION TO DISMISS

I.      OPERATING AGREEMENT, SCHEDULE 1, SECTION 1.8.2 AND COMMISSION
        PRECEDENT PRECLUDE MON POWER’S REQUESTED RETROACTIVE
        RELIEF

        The Commission should dismiss the Complaint because its request for retroactive relief is

precluded by PJM’s Tariff. Operating Agreement Schedule 1, section 1.8.2, provides that disputes

concerning PJM’s dispatch decisions should be made directly to PJM, not to the Commission.

Section 1.8.2(a) specifically states that “Market Participants shall comply with all determinations

of the Office of the Interconnection on the selection, scheduling or dispatch of resources in the

PJM Interchange Energy Market, or to meet the operational requirements of the PJM Region.” 50

Further, “[c]omplaints arising from or relating to such determinations shall be brought to the

attention of [PJM].” 51 Section 1.8.2(d) provides that PJM’s Market Participants shall not be

entitled to any “actual, compensatory, consequential or punitive damages, opportunity costs, or

other form of reimbursement from [PJM] or any other Market Participant for any loss, liability or

       The strength of the law on this subject is made even more clear when considering the

Commission decision leading up to the landmark D.C. Circuit decision in ODEC. There, the

Commission found that it lacks “any power to disregard on equitable grounds either the filed rate

Day-ahead Market that exceeded $1,000 MW per hour. 59 Thus, Old Dominion had to temporarily

sell energy capacity at a loss. Despite the injury to Old Dominion, both the Commission and the

D.C. Circuit concluded that the Tariff provided no remedy. 60 To the contrary, “the filed Tariff
